en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming, Song Dynasty. II.

From "At that time" onwards is the second major section, the *Zhengzongfen* (Main Body of the Teaching), which has two parts: first, a general presentation of the text’s meaning; second, [the specific analysis].
Regarding the first, showing the beginning and end of the scripture: it includes the three chapters in their entirety—<Repentance>, <Praise>, and <The Chapter on Emptiness>—as well as...
This half-chapter on "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*) is likewise part of the formal teaching (*samyag-deśanā*).
Second, from "In general, three... onwards, there is the analysis of the great meaning of the three chapters, in two parts:
first, the citation of other masters; second... [text continues].
First, the explicit clarification of the other's position, in three parts:
first, the account of the first master;
second, from "The second says" onwards, the account of the next master, in two parts:
First, the introduction;
second, from "Next then" onwards, Zhizhe (Zhang’an) refutes [the previous view].
Since the current text does not mention the Master [Huisi] or Tiantai, we know this is a private refutation.

Although emptiness is the Middle Way, it is the Middle Way employed at the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) to destroy attachments; it is not yet the essence of the Middle Way manifested at the stage of the fruit (*phala*).
Although the dharmas themselves do not differ, their functions and the meanings they manifest are distinct.
Since the ancients were ignorant of this, we do not follow them here.
III. Below "The Three Pitakas" (Tripiṭaka), the True Meaning (Paramārtha) is described in two parts:
first, the description.

Regarding "empty space" and so forth, the new translation’s *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*), in the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies," states: "The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha: [and so forth].
"How does a bodhisattva practice in accordance with the Dharma regarding the profound secrets of all Tathāgatas?
This refers to the introductory narrative.
Second, from "It is simply... onwards, Zhangan refutes it.
In every section of the various sutras there are questions posed; how could they all be fully cited and recounted?
Therefore, it is said that their meaning is weak.
Second, from "The Master says" onwards, the present master selects and discards [the material].

Although that *Ākāśagarbha* [Sūtra] addresses the question in terms of causes, the Buddha’s answer states that all Tathāgatas possess the three bodies (*trikāya*); is this not, then, the meaning of the fruit?
Therefore, one should set aside the third school and adopt the first.
The preceding Master may be understood.
Second, from "New and Old" onwards, the present intention is clarified in three parts:
first, clarifying the essence and substance according to the new sutra, in three sub-sections: [The text continues with the subsequent sub-sections.]

First, the four Buddhas explained the traces (*jì*) to reveal the source (*běn*), sweeping away doubts regarding the brevity of eighty years and clarifying the long-term response that is like a drop in the ocean.

Having heard that these responsive manifestations can be both long and short, one realizes that the Dharma-body and Reward-body are neither extinguished nor born. Once the source and the trace are thus integrated, all conceptual thought comes to an end.
Those of superior capacity, upon merely hearing its traces, also awaken to its fundamental source;
this corresponds to the first turning of the wheel.
Second, from the words "If [they] have not yet," the Prince reveals the fundamental to enable the awakening to the traces.

In the "Chapter on the Lifespan" of the new sutra, after the four Buddhas had finished speaking of how their lifespans benefit sentient beings, there was a brahmin named Kauṇḍinya who, desiring to be reborn in heaven, sought a portion of the Buddha’s relics as small as a mustard seed.
Prince Kṛkī replied with a verse, saying:
"Even if the legs of a mosquito could be used to construct a city tower, there would still be no relics from the Tathāgata’s tranquil body."

To ascend from the earth to heaven by means of a ladder made of rabbit horns—such a thing is impossible; likewise, there is no such basis for merit in those who harbor wrong thoughts regarding the Buddha’s relics.

That a mouse might climb a ladder of rabbit horns, eat the moon, and destroy the asuras—such a thing is possible; yet that one could rely on the relics to exhaust all delusions and attain liberation—there is no such basis for this.

Those of middling capacity directly hear that the principle of the Dharmakāya is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, and thereby awaken to the fact that the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya can be both permanent and impermanent.
Once principle and phenomena are thus harmonized, conceptual thought is utterly transcended.
In the second week as well.
Third, from "If [the disciples] have not yet... onwards, Śākyamuni discusses both aspects together so that they may understand them simultaneously.

Since those of inferior capacity are dull-witted, they cannot immediately comprehend the meaning of the mutual fusion between the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku) through a one-sided discussion; therefore, Śākyamuni fully expounds the three bodies, namely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Just as lightning exists dependent on the sky and light exists dependent on lightning, the *dharmakāya* is principle (*li*) and the *saṃbhogakāya* is wisdom (*zhi*).

Since wisdom accords with principle, it gives rise to the *nirmāṇakāya*. The three bodies are in profound unity; though one, they are not fixed as one, yet the three bodies remain distinct. Therefore, the title of this chapter is "The Differentiation of the Three Bodies."

The Dharma-body is the fundamental essence, while the transformation bodies are its manifestations; when these are taught simultaneously, wondrous understanding arises and all conceptual deliberation ceases.
This occurs during the third week.
These three cycles all expound the Tathāgata’s doctrine of permanence to reveal the essence, intending to cause those who hear them to give rise to wisdom and realize the principle.
Second, in the "Chapter on Repentance" (Chānpǐn) below, it is judged that all three chapters clarify the function (*yòng*).
The essence of the Buddha’s wisdom reveals the substance of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); this is precisely what is termed the essence of the sūtra and the substance of the sūtra.

All sentient beings take this essence of the school as their fundamental mind; if they can perform repentance and praise, and cultivate the two kinds of emptiness, then the Buddha’s wondrous function will arise in its entirety, causing these sentient beings to extinguish evil and give rise to good, and further developing the function of emptiness to guide them toward the fulfillment of the two functions. Therefore, it is said that all three grades are the functioning of the sutra.
3. Below the phrase "of the present," it clarifies that there are two versions of this fundamental text:

the extensive and the abbreviated. Since both versions manifest the three bodies (trikāya), and what is manifested in this current abbreviated version is no different, Master Kumārajīva—conforming to the disposition of those who prefer brevity—did not translate the latter two [sections].
2. From "The text as... below, the text is divided and explained in four parts;
the first part has two sections:
first, the division of the text.
2. Explanation, in four parts:
first, the verses spoken by the four Buddhas, in two parts:
first, the introduction by the narrator of the sutra.
II. The Four Buddhas’ Exposition of Similes, in two parts:
A. An Analysis of the Body and the Teaching, in two parts:
1. The Question.
2. The Response, in two parts:
First, the clarification of the teaching.
Originally, it was designated according to the capacity of the audience; there is no distinction between the common and the particular.
Second, the section beginning with "The vision also" clarifies the body [of the Buddha].
Regarding the interpretation of the title and the classification of the teaching, this sutra belongs to the Shared Teaching (p'ung-chiao).
This teaching clarifies that the Buddha’s sixteen-foot body and the Honored Unique Body (tsun-tê) are perceived differently by different people; therefore, it is called the "combined body" (ho-shen).

Now, within this chamber there is an assembly of those belonging to the three vehicles; among them, those bodhisattvas of sharp faculties are able to deeply contemplate emptiness and perceive the principle of non-emptiness.
This principle of non-emptiness is precisely the fact that all sentient beings and Buddhas share the same awakened nature.

Therefore, although one sees the Buddha, the Buddha does not come from without; whether great or small, all are without boundary. Thus it is said that the four Buddhas share the same *viśeṣa-kāya* (exalted body); their body, wisdom, and functional application are one and eternal. How could this apply only to the Buddhas being non-dual and without distinction?
Their disciples are likewise no different from them; thus it is said that "the assembly is one.
Although the distinction between [the primary] opening and [the secondary] cessation has not yet been revealed, those who benefit others perceive them as identical.

However, for dull-witted bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles, since they perceive only emptiness, when they see the four Buddhas coming from outside, they grasp at their physical forms and boundaries as being merely transformational manifestations (*nirmāṇakāya*). If even the Buddhas are distinct from one another, how could their disciples be the same?
Because there are distinctions among the three vehicles, it is said that they are "numerous.
Second, from "dividing into eight" onwards, the text is divided to explain its meaning, in two parts:
first, an account of how two schools divide the text.
2. Regarding the section beginning with "The old [translation] says," the interpretation provided by the first master has four parts:
first, the establishment of analogies through four verses, which has two sub-sections;
first, the refutation of the ancients, which has two further sub-sections: ...
First, the introduction;
second, from "This meaning" onwards, the refutation.
Because the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma is unerring throughout the three periods [of time], it is good in the beginning, middle, and end.
Because it can express the existence of dharmas, its language is skillful;
because that which is expressed is free from emotional attachment, its meaning is profound and far-reaching.
If one were to equate this with the absence of intention, how could one ever awaken to the doctrine of permanence?
Therefore, we know that the ancient masters were entirely mistaken regarding the intent of the sutra.
Second, "Now, as for 'provisionally composed'... and below is the present explanation, which has two parts:

first, opening the chapters and stating the intent; second, [the detailed exposition]. Within the first part, there are two sections: (1) opening the chapters and stating the intent; (2) [the detailed exposition].
First, the opening of the chapter.
The meaning explained by the Great Master is inexhaustible; however, interpreting the text according to the capacities of his audience, he demonstrates three points of intent.
Second, from "The Four Truths" onwards, the exposition of the intent, which has two parts:
First, the three causes and effects are clarified.
The Four Truths are the principle, upon which both cause and effect depend;
the Four Mindfulnesses are the practice, cultivated within the causal stage.
The four virtues are inherently present, yet their realization occurs in the fruit.
Without these three meanings, the doctrine of permanence cannot be manifested.
Second, from "If one discusses... onwards, the causes for the three marks are clarified.
The realization of the fruit arises from the cause, and cause and fruit arise from the truths; if one wishes to establish cause and fruit, the understanding of the truths must come first.
Second, "From 'above this'... and below, the meaning is explained according to the chapters, in three parts:
first, the explanation based on the Four Noble Truths, in two parts: [The subsequent sections follow.]
First, the explanation of the verse by means of the Four Noble Truths, in two parts:
first, a preliminary exposition of the meaning of the truths, in two parts;
first, clarifying the meaning of the four truths, in three parts:
First, regarding the clarification of the object and the wisdom in contrast to the preceding section:
the preceding section clarified the person who speaks, which appropriately corresponds to wisdom;
the present section clarifies the Dharma that is spoken, which corresponds to principle (*li*).
2. Regarding the section "Old Readings" (*jùdú*) below, this refutes the ancient view that [the Buddha] only performed these deeds in his final life.
As for what is called "reading the text," it refers to the passage in the third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explaining the title "Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Therefore, the treatise asks:
"What is right and universal knowledge?
It answers:
"Knowing suffering, [knowing it] as the characteristic of suffering," and so forth.

When reading this passage, although the character "ru" (如) was interpreted as meaning "not different," the distinction between the Tripiṭaka’s definition of "not different" as knowing phenomena in accordance with principle, and the Mahāyāna’s definition of "not different" as knowing phenomena as being identical to principle, was obscured. Consequently, the interpretation of the meaning remained confined solely to the level of phenomena, failing entirely to reveal the underlying principle.

Furthermore, this passage explains "Perfect and Universal Knowledge" (*samyaksambodhi*): "perfect knowledge" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and "universal knowledge" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Third, from "Now, to clarify" onwards, the correct doctrine of the present master is elucidated in two parts:
first, by means of the two truths;...
Second, regarding the three truths.

The meaning of the two interpretations is as follows: since the four [truths] beginning with suffering constitute the objects of cause and effect within both the mundane and supramundane realms, if one does not realize that these four objects are simultaneously the True and the Conventional, as well as Emptiness, the Provisional, and the Middle, they cannot be called "truths. Rather, one must realize the two truths by taking the Middle as the True.

The intent of emptiness and conventionality in the Three Treatises lies within the Truths; one must perceive that within each and every phenomenon of the causes and effects of the ten realms—whether in delusion or enlightenment—all dharmas are without activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), only then can they be called the "permanence of worldly characteristics."
The principle is not otherwise; by what means, then, could one dispel the doubts of those with faithful characteristics?
The two phrases both first explain based on the Truth of Suffering and secondly conclude by applying the same to the remaining truths.
Second, from "Clarifying Consciousness" onwards, it clarifies the intention regarding the [Four] Truths.
2. From "All" onwards, the text is explained by means of the Truths (satya).

4. Regarding the sequence where cause precedes and effect follows, the elements of water, earth, mountain, and space are correlated with the Truths of Accumulation, Suffering, Path, and Cessation respectively; each is likewise divided into three parts:
first, the citation and indication.
Second, citing scriptural evidence;
third, explaining the conclusion.
Regarding the citation from the *Shorter Prajñā* within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), this refers to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other such texts are termed "small" based on their textual length; however, in terms of principle, they are identical to the great [Prajñāpāramitā] treatises.
In those [texts], Mount Sumeru is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s body.
Now, the meaning of "accumulation" (*cita*) regarding the realization of suffering is the same; it is not something produced by the cause of origination (*samudaya*).

However, using the Buddha’s *vipākaphala* (fruition of maturation) to realize the *janmaphala* (fruition of birth) serves to manifest that suffering is unconditioned (*akṛtaka*), that the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all suchness (*tathatā*), and that there is no suffering to be abandoned, because birth itself is generated as cessation.
"Pan-zhi" (盤峙) means "pan-hui" (盤迴).
"Zhi" (峙) means "standing.
Some write it as the character "pan" (磐), which is an error.
Regarding the citation of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "ground of wisdom" (*jñāna-bhūmi*) within the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), the "ground" is used as a metaphor for the ground itself.
Having reached the ground of wisdom is the very essence of the Path.

As for the two routes—by water and by land—the land route reaches only this shore of the ocean; it may be likened to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) practicing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which, not having yet crossed over the *pariṇāma-vipariṇāma-śakti* (the power of transformation), still remain on this shore.

Just as a waterway can reach the further shore of the ocean, so too may the distinct cultivation of the path-factors within the One Vehicle lead one to immediately reach the shore of the Three Virtues beyond the two types of death.

Regarding the citation from the *Lotus Sūtra* within the context of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), it uses emptiness to illustrate emptiness; since this emptiness is ultimate, it is said that "one ultimately returns [to it]."
The five obscurations are smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and the hand of the asuras.
The three luminaries are the sun, the moon, and the stars.
The principle of cessation is eternally present and fundamentally unobscured; even now, it is not something newly purified.
Question:
If the Buddha-body is likened to a mountain, the Path to the ground, and Cessation to the void—
since these three constitute teachings that accord with principle, it is possible to discuss the Dharma-body as that which is realized.

If, in the initial exposition of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the citations and explanations address only afflictions (*kleśa*), how could they also be called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?
Answer:

Within each of the four unconditioned truths (*asaṃskṛta-dharmas*), there is the Middle Way (*madhyama*). If it were not the case that all things converge within affliction, what then would be called the Middle?
Because it is precisely the Middle Way, suffering is called the Dharma-body, the Path is the ground of wisdom, and cessation is called wondrous emptiness.
Thus one should know that by directly using afflictions to explain the origin of suffering and thereby revealing the Dharma-body, the intention is most subtle; let the practitioner understand this.
II. Clarifying the Four Truths to Resolve Doubts, in two parts:
A. Showing the Principle to Clarify the Severing of Doubt, in two parts:
1. Showing the Principle to Clarify the Characteristics.

The above explains the general auspicious signs: all unprecedented events throughout the entire world appear in their full manifestation, signifying that the provisional and real environments and rewards of the ten realms all reveal the three virtues.

Now, it is clarified that within each of the ten realms—whether provisional or real, primary or secondary—the four truths and the three virtues are present in every instance. This principle pervading all phenomena is called the Dharma-body; knowing this is called the Reward-body, and the arising of its function is called the Response-body. These response-bodies may be long or short.
II. From "The Aspect of Faith" (*śraddhā-nimitta*) onwards, the aspect of severing doubt is shown, in three parts:
first, the doubt to be severed;
second, from "The Four Buddhas" onwards, the teaching that severs it.
Regarding the four analogies, they were originally intended to clarify that [the Buddha] should live long; the Great Master specifically explained them through the Four Noble Truths.
If it were not the case that his lifespan was entirely the Dharmakāya and that the three bodies are one essence, how could he so wonderfully reconcile the two explanations in the Commentary?
Therefore, it was previously stated that "the words are skillful and the meaning is profound.
If [the body] were definitively compared to a single person, how could the words be considered skillful?
If the three [aspects] were entirely distinct from one another, how could the meaning be considered profound?
Third, "The Response to the Exhortation" below praises the skillfulness of his intention.
Although the text and metaphors should be extensive, the meaning here clarifies the Dharma of retribution.
Xinxiang (Faith-Aspect) attained the intended meaning, and the darkness of his doubts was suddenly dispelled.
2. From "Explaining this" onwards, there is the praise and explanation of the wondrous exhortation to reflect.
Through the skillful metaphors of the four Buddhas, the doubts of Śraddhālakṣaṇa are severed;
through the wondrous explanations of the wise, the understanding of the practitioner is inspired.
Now that you have encountered this, how could you not reflect upon it with careful scrutiny?
Second, from the "Four Verses" onwards, the explanation is given in terms of the four mindfulnesses (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Mindfulness" refers here to the three sublime contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.
The "abodes" refer to the four sublime objects of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*).
If these were not the objects of contemplation, the three bodies (*trikāya*) would not be manifested; how then could this be called a discourse on permanence?
This explanation consists of three parts:
First, the correlation of the verses with the Dharma has three parts.
First, abandoning the specific for the general:
since body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are merely the five aggregates, one knows that the four foundations of mindfulness originally reside within the Truth of Suffering.

However, while the cultivation of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) applies to all four teachings, here we restrict ourselves to the Perfect Teaching alone. This means that contemplating the body as pure, impure, or neither pure nor impure—and likewise contemplating phenomena (dharma) as self, non-self, or neither self nor non-self—all result in the realization of the three truths.
2. From "All" below, the explanation proceeds by way of general correspondence.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness of perception and formations: these are simply the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas, which subsumes these two aggregates;
however, since they are now being assigned to the stages (bhūmi), the names of the aggregates are retained.

Regarding "the practitioner of perception and grasping": perception grasps at characteristics, while formations (*saṃskāra*) are shifting and flowing; therefore, it is called "the practice of formations.
The second character for "practice" (*xing*) in this compound is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*).
Third, the section beginning with "If one contemplates... explains the reason for the verse.
The causes and conditions for eternal life cannot be accomplished without the perfect foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); therefore, the following verse is employed as a counterpart.
Second, from "If one contemplates" onwards, the doubt regarding the Dharma is resolved in two parts:
first, clarifying the causes and conditions of the foundations of mindfulness; second... [text continues].
First, the characteristics of cultivating the causes:

the four aspects of withering are emptiness, the four aspects of flourishing are the provisional, and the double negation is the Middle; though there is a sequential order in their exposition, there is no temporal succession in their cultivation—this is the threefold contemplation within a single mind.
Therefore, the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa between the four withered and four flourishing twin trees precisely symbolizes this.
Second, from "The accomplishment of the five" [onward] is the aspect of attaining the fruit, which has three parts:
first, clarifying the aspect of the fusion and identity of the three virtues.

To wither and flourish simultaneously—this is the practice of a single kṣaṇa that is neither withering nor flourishing. With moment-to-moment perfect mindfulness never ceasing, one passes through the five grades and gives rise to what resembles the realization of truth. Upon reaching the stage of fruition, the three delusions are completely purified; the five aggregates across the ten realms are sovereign and unimpeded, which is called the fivefold liberation.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the hundred realms are pure like space; this is called the five *prajñās*.
The five aggregates of the hundred realms are ultimately inconceivable; this is called the five *dharmakāyas*.
Wisdom merges with the five aggregates, and principle (*li*) is that which is merged with; therefore, it is termed "principle."
Although the essence is one, it is undivided yet divided.
Prajñā is that which is in accord, and the Dharmakāya is that with which there is accord; because they are in accord through their characteristics, the function of liberation arises.
The passage beginning with "Although there are three" clarifies the meaning of the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*), as is commonly explained.
Second, from "The Benevolent Kings" (*Renwang*) onwards, the constant nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is clarified.

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means that which does not change; thus, the eight phases of the five aggregates within the hundred realms do not shift, pervading the ten directions. However, it is not that there exists a separate "nature-aggregate" apart from the phenomena themselves; rather, the very substance of the aggregates of good and evil, the defiled aggregates, and so forth, are themselves eternally abiding. This is termed the "dharma-nature aggregate."
Be careful not to seek it elsewhere.
Third, following the phrase "the concealment of," the text clarifies the characteristics of the essence and function of the three bodies.
Being neither [identical to nor different from] the Dharma-body and Reward-body, the entire essence gives rise to its function, capable of being both permanent and impermanent.

Regarding the statement that "if used frequently, they become long," etc.: if they were long, there would be four analogies; if short, eighty. Since both should be considered as having a fixed lifespan, they are all impermanent.
Now, to distinguish between permanence and impermanence based on length: it is because measures such as the *śaila* (mountain-weight) can manifest permanence.
If the essence were not eternal, how could it cause those who respond to it—humans and devas alike—to be beyond counting?
Therefore, when Śraddhālakṣaṇa heard that the Buddha’s life span was eighty years, he doubted that the lifespan was eternal;
yet upon hearing the four parables of longevity, he realized the eternally abiding essence.
Therefore it is said: "If used constantly, it is long; if not used constantly, it is short.
Second, from the section on "Faithful Aspect" (*śraddhālakṣaṇa*) below, the fruit-function is used to resolve doubts, in three parts:
first, the doubt to be refuted; [the remaining two parts follow].
Second, from "The Four Buddhas" downward, is the method for destroying [delusion];
third, from "Faithful Appearance" downward, is the sign of attaining understanding.
These three sections, when directed toward the Four Noble Truths to resolve doubts, do not differ in their underlying intent; nevertheless, they must be investigated deeply.
III. Below the "Four Verses," there is an explanation based on the four virtues, in two parts:
first, matching the verses to the virtues.
If even the earth ground, when crushed into dust, lacks any mark of purity, how could impurity still exist?
Therefore, in contrast to the purity of virtue, it is illustrated by the principle that purity purifies both the pure and the defiled.
Second, from "The Four Virtues" onwards, the doubts are resolved through the virtues, in two parts:
first, revealing the function of the virtues.
Regarding the four virtues of permanence and so forth, the student must discern that while their names are identical, their natures are distinct.
First, the permanence, bliss, self, and purity to which ordinary beings are attached have as their substance the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Second, the permanence, bliss, self, and purity established by Bodhisattvas have as their substance ignorance (*avidyā*).
The three Buddhas’ realization of permanence, bliss, self, and purity has as its essence the Middle Way;
now, since all four [aspects] are the Middle, they are each revealed through "double negation. In principle, this must negate the twelve inversions.

Now, these qualities such as permanence and so forth share the same essence despite having different names from "neither impermanent nor non-impermanent" and so on. The four virtues that are a dual negation are the Dharma-body; the four capacities that are the profound union with wisdom are the Reward-body.

Since the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are thus in profound accord, they can respond to phenomena by manifesting the spontaneous application of the sovereign functions of permanence and impermanence, and ultimate purity and impurity.
Second, from the section on "Faithful Appearance" (*Śraddhālakṣaṇa*) onwards, there is the removal of doubts, which is threefold:
first, the doubt to be dispelled; [the remaining two parts follow].
Second, from "The Four Buddhas" downward, is the method capable of destroying [doubt];
third, from "Faithful Appearance" downward, is the sign of attaining understanding.
If one understands the intent of severing doubt through the Four Noble Truths, these three sections become clear.
2. Regarding the single verse beginning with "one hundred koṭis," there are two parts to the combined analogy:

first, the presentation of the two errors in the ancient interpretation; second, from "the old [masters] say" onwards, the clarification of the present intention to refute the ancient view, which has two sub-sections: 1. The presentation of the two errors in the ancient interpretation. 2. From "the old [masters] say" onwards, the clarification of the present intention to refute the ancient view, which has two sub-sections: [The text continues with the specific points of refutation.]
First, refuting misconceptions regarding the literal text, in two parts:
first, presenting the ancient interpretations.
The ancients merely aligned the text word-for-word, failing to understand the intended meaning behind the four Buddhas' skillful demonstrations.
2. Showing the present intent, in two parts:
first, showing the profound meaning of the sutra.
The four metaphors have a limited scope, and "hundreds of thousands" is a mere number; who does not know this?
Sudatta raised [the example] by means of measure and number; how much more so for that which is immeasurable and incalculable?
Second, from the words "Since you... onwards, he refutes ancient misinterpretations of the sutras.

This statement contains both concession and refutation: it concedes that one may understand the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) through transformation, while refuting the delusion regarding the dharma of retribution.

The Dharma of retribution is the very essence of the responsive transformation; yet those with shallow understanding of profound texts ruin themselves and others. Having already incurred transgressions themselves, they cause others to slander the Teaching.
Second, the refutation of biased attachments regarding meaning.

"Meaning" refers to that which is elucidated: the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). These three bodies each possess four propositions—namely, permanence, impermanence, both, and neither—which reveal that the three and the one cannot be conceived or described as being either identical or different.

The Explanation Based on the Definitions of the Characters has two parts: [the definition of the first character and the definition of the second character]. Regarding the first:
First, the explanation of the *chān* (repentance), in two parts:
first, clarifying the seeking of a mirror.
*Nǜ* (恧) is pronounced with the initial *nú* and the final *liù*; it means shame (*cán*).
Second, from "The body is covered" onwards, it clarifies being reflected upon.
Second, the explanation of repentance has two parts:
first, clarifying that which can be abandoned; [the rest follows].
Second, explaining that which is abolished.

The meaning of "abolishing ten" is as follows: the mind is like a sovereign, while body and speech are like ministers. Since the sovereign has mastered himself, the ministers cease their violence; thus, the ten items are collectively abolished.
2. From "Furthermore, another method" below, the various types are explained by way of the Dharma-gates.
2. From "Repentance" below, the three kinds of repentance are clarified, in three parts:
first, clarifying the three kinds of appearances, in two parts: [text continues].
First, listing the names to indicate [the subject].
Three types of names are listed to show that the phenomena [discussed] are common to both the Great and Small Vehicles.
Second, from "The Small Vehicle" onwards, there is an explanation based on characteristics, which has two parts:
First, the initial procedure for the minor triad is explained.
*Vinaya* is translated here as "Discipline" (*lǜ*).
Regarding the "twenty monks," this refers specifically to the assembly required for the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
However, there are four methods of remediation.
First, the remedy for concealing one's mental transgressions, which refers to practicing *parivāsa*.
This is translated as "concealment" (*pūrvavāsana*) or "separate dwelling" (*pi-li-zhu*); it means residing separately in a single room and not being permitted to dwell together with the Saṃgha.
If one enters among the assembly, one must neither engage in discussion nor provide answers.
One who practices this method must complete one hundred days; because it is impossible to remember the original number of days of concealment, the limit is set at one hundred days.

2. The expiation for the offense of concealment (*praticchādana*): This refers to the fact that having committed an offense, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) if it is concealed, and a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) if it is not concealed.
If the offense was concealed, one must first repent for the *dukkaṭa* and subsequently undergo the period of *parivāsa* (probation).
Third, the expiation for offenses involving mental transgressions of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class, which consists of practicing the *mānatva* penance for six nights—this is translated as "mental joy.
Although one has already rejoiced in one's own mind, this also causes the community of monks to rejoice.
Because of his previous joy, he was granted a short period of time—specifically six nights—and thus it is called "joy of mind.
The Saṃgha rejoiced, saying:
"This person has repented and become pure."
Therefore, it is said that "the community of monks rejoices.

Fourth, regarding the treatment of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: this refers to the removal of guilt through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) within an assembly of twenty monks.

However, if the offense was concealed, one must not undergo the *mānatva* penance directly without passing through the transition of the dawn; rather, one must first perform the *mānatva* and only then enter the assembly for the removal of guilt.

Regarding the practice of performing the rite every half-month: this refers to when one is undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation); at each half-monthly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one must inform the community of monks, saying, "I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Regarding the ritual performed before another person (*pratideśanā*), this refers to the confession of heavy offenses (*sthūlātyaya*).
Regarding the "reproving the mind" (*cittavipratisāra*), this refers to the confession of light offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
The *Māyī-śāstra* states: "For intentional acts, one performs a single recitation before another person."
Regarding those who have committed errors, they should take responsibility for their own minds and repent.

Although there are methods for repentance even for those in the Hīnayāna who have committed a *pārājika* offense, the commentary does not cite them because, once the repentance is completed, the individual remains a *śrāmaṇera* undergoing training; since they still obstruct the attainment of the holy fruits, this does not accord with the principle here of restoring one's original purity.
Therefore, Jingxi said:
"Minor offenses, once regretted, have already obstructed the fruit; yet they still constitute grave transgressions that have not been forgotten.
Second, from "Āgama" onwards, [the section on] grasping at marks.

The preceding section clarified the performance of rituals, which merely requires that the three karmas accord with the Buddha’s regulations; thus, when the rite is completed, the offense is extinguished.
Yet, this still involves a distracted mind, so the extinction of the offense remains superficial.
Now, we discuss the grasping of signs, which pertains to a concentrated mind; when the visualization is perfected and the sign arises, the extinction of the offense is profound.
Therefore, when the perception of the snake’s mouth is established, how could it merely eliminate the sin of lust?
It also causes the desire-mind not to arise.
Third, from "There is also" onwards, is non-arising (*anutpāda*).
To speak of "contemplating emptiness" means to analyze phenomena to clarify their emptiness.

One contemplates that the mind which creates transgressions has no inherent sovereign from the beginning; every thought-moment is impermanent. There is no one who can act, nor is there such a thing as karmic retribution. Once the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) is extinguished, all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are forever stilled.
If this contemplation is perfected, the four miserable destinies will be eliminated, and one must emerge from the three realms.
The three types of repentance in the Hīnayāna are briefly characterized as follows.
Second, the explanation of the Mahāyāna, in three parts:
First, the method of practice;
second, grasping the signs;
third, non-arising.
The practitioner should know that there are three types of repentance methods: non-arising is the primary, while the other two serve as auxiliary conditions.

Therefore, the previous commentary states: "Ash-water and soapberries assist clear water; if the wondrous contemplation is lacking, it is not called Mahāyāna, but is instead like the fruitless asceticism of the non-Buddhists."

One must first approach a virtuous teacher to learn the place for repentance and the method of repentance before one may perform the rituals and ceremonies of the *dojō*; therefore, in all matters, one should employ wondrous contemplation to guide them, ensuring that the performance of rites and other practices accord with ultimate reality and become entirely causes for Buddhahood.

Some claim that the methods practiced at the site of enlightenment (daochang) involve ritual procedures, asserting that one must first cultivate the six dharmas within the ten vehicles before subsequently assisting in the opening [of the Dharma]; yet they fail to consider that the former six [vehicles] are utilized within the site of enlightenment itself.
Now, in this clear exposition of repentance, all three types are fully discussed;

how could one possibly abandon the practice of ritual action? Furthermore, there is a single fascicle of the *Fahua Samādhi* that circulates separately in the world, established by the Great Master specifically for beginners to repent of offenses that obstruct the Path, so that they may subsequently cultivate various dhyānas and samādhis.

Furthermore, regarding the various gateways of asceticism and diligence, each may be practiced according to one's inclination; these may be cultivated by a beginner, provided that all such practices take the perfect contemplation of non-arising as their primary guide. By ensuring that every single practice is itself this very nature—characterized by no cultivation and no attainment—one achieves perfect practice.

Is it that all practices of the wondrous contemplation, the wondrous objects, and the wondrous cultivation—such as the arousal of the great mind and the settling of the mind—are entirely wondrous cultivation?
If this were so, then within the "following one's own intention" (suizuyi), which traverses those three natures, there would be no ten vehicles at all; how then could it be called samādhi?
If you have not yet mastered this yourself, you should rely on a virtuous friend to provide guidance and exhortation in your practice; only then will it bring profound benefit.

Furthermore, you must understand that although the last of the three Mahāyāna repentances may be practiced independently, if progress is not made, one must rely on the first two; nor can the first two ever be separated from the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Having attained this understanding, one may then proceed to explain the practice of the three types of repentance.
First, the ritual method (*dharmakarma*).

Regarding the "eight hundred days" and so forth, the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* states: "One who knows the Dharma further instructs [the practitioner] to smear the latrine for eight hundred days, declaring each day:..."
"You have committed an impure act; therefore, with single-minded devotion, smear and repair all latrines so that no one knows of it.
Once you have finished smearing them, bathe, pay homage to the thirty-five Buddhas, and invoke the name of Ākāśagarbha."
"Prostrate yourself before the twelve divisions of the scriptures and confess your transgressions," and so forth.
Regarding the "ninety days" and so on, the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra* states: "There are four things by which one quickly attains this samādhi:
first, for three months, one must not harbor worldly thoughts for even as long as the snap of a finger."
Second, one must not lie down for even as long as it takes to snap one's fingers during the three months.
Third, one must not rest nor sit while practicing *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) for the three months, except for the brief intervals before and after meals.
"Fourth, when preaching the sutras for others, one must not hope for clothing or food from them; these are the four.
*Pratyutpanna* is translated here as "Buddha-standing.
When this samādhi is accomplished, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in mid-air; therefore, it is named "Buddha-standing."
Regarding the phrase "Ash-water Bath" (Kaidō), it clarifies that each of the aforementioned ritual practices purifies the three karmas.

Regarding the phrase "Chanting while Turning" (Junsu), each dharma has its own established regulations; among these, the regulation for chanting while turning the scriptures according to the Vaipulya (Hōdō) is most essential.

Circumambulate one hundred and twenty times, reciting the *dhāraṇī* of the *Tantu* one hundred and twenty times; with each circumambulation and each recitation, proceed neither too slowly nor too quickly.
Having finished the circumambulation, sit back down and contemplate the Middle Way and true emptiness.
Because this ritual procedure guides one [toward awakening], it is called "the performance of the rite" (*dharmaprayoga*).
Second, "taking the signs.

Regarding the twelve dreams of the king, the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "First, seek auspicious dreams; there are twelve kinds in total. If you obtain even one sign, then repentance is permitted."
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If one violates any of the ten precepts, one should be taught to perform repentance until a 'good sign' (*lakṣaṇa*) is seen.
Good signs include the Buddha coming to stroke one's head, or seeing light, flowers, and so forth; upon this, the transgression is extinguished."

Regarding the phrase "proclaiming the sound" below: that sutra clarifies that if, within a dream or during seated meditation, this bodhisattva appears to the practitioner, seals their arm with a *maṇi* jewel seal, forms the characters for "extinguishing transgressions," or they hear the sound of "transgressions extinguished"—when such signs arise, one knows that their transgressions will certainly be extinguished.

The phrase "although not" [refers to] being within the *maṇḍala*; it is not that one does not perform the ritual acts (*dharmakriyā*), for both [the internal and external aspects] are established based on excellence and are termed "grasping signs.
What is called "functional activity" refers to the performance of the ritual acts.
Third, non-arising:
because there is no reality of the offenses in each successive thought-moment, the thought and the reality—though distinguished by the names of subject and object—are non-dual in essence.
To contemplate in this way, the characteristics of the offenses are forgotten and the reality itself also vanishes.
This wisdom is like the sun, dissolving the frost and dew of transgressions.
It takes no object as its condition; it is ultimately empty and devoid of the characteristics of center or periphery. Since this principle is beyond reproach, it is called supreme.

Below the phrase "although not," these three types of repentance are cultivated simultaneously; the realization of non-arising is the primary practice, while the other two serve as auxiliary conditions, which is why it is said that they "combine both."
This is the practice of the primary and auxiliary combined as one; like adding oil to a lamp, it makes the light brighter, and the realization of principle becomes even more rapid.
Second, "The Ritual Procedure" (*zuo-fa*) and below clarifies the three types of efficacy, in two parts:
first, the direct demonstration of the efficacy; second... [text continues].
First, the clarification of the eradication of evil, in two parts:
the first four sections provide a general explanation applicable to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

It is said to be "applicable to both" because these four sections explain the three types of repentance; although the underlying intent lies in the Mahāyāna, the specific characteristics that distinguish it from the Hīnayāna have not yet been manifested. Thus, the eradication of evil is unimpeded in the teachings of both vehicles, which is why it is called "applicable to both."
Among these four, the first explains [the nature of offenses] by way of excluding their essential nature; it has three parts.
First, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding "unmanifested offenses" (*avijñapti-pāpa*): when one formerly received the Buddha’s precepts, the essence of the unmanifested arises by virtue of the ritual procedure; if one violates them, one incurs the offense of contravention.
Now, by means of this ritual procedure, one reverses and destroys these offenses.
As for what are called "natural offenses" (prakṛti-sāvadya), they refer to the ten non-virtuous actions;
regardless of whether one has formally undertaken the precepts or not, the nature of committing them is inherently an offense.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of an offense," the *Śāstra* states: "If one cuts down large grass or kills an animal, the two offenses are confessed together; both types of transgressions against the regulations are removed, yet the requirement to compensate for the life of the killed animal remains."
2. Grasping the sign (*nimitta-grāha*).

By means of the mental image formed through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the power of cultivation is so strong that it can transform evil karma; therefore, it is able to extinguish both the natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) offenses.

Regarding the phrase "like a replacement" below: the branches and leaves metaphorically represent the nature of prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), while the root metaphorically represents ignorance (*avidyā*).
As long as the delusions of the mind persist, offenses can be repeatedly committed, just as branches and leaves continue to grow.

Since ignorance has already been distinguished as being of the nature of negation (*pratiṣedha*), this ignorance thus extends both within and beyond the realms; this is precisely its characteristic common to the Hīnayāna.
Third, non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore" explains [the cessation of offenses] in terms of the three trainings.
Because one employs ritual procedures (*vidhi*) to prevent wrongdoing, one extinguishes the offense of transgression against the precepts;
because one focuses the mind by grasping the characteristics [of the object], one extinguishes the offense of transgression against concentration.
By contemplating non-arising, one extinguishes the faults of wisdom.
Transgressions regarding phenomena are the faults of the precepts; mental distraction is the fault of meditative concentration; and delusive darkness is the fault of wisdom.
3. Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore, it also acts": this explains the removal of the three retributions.
Although both [the obstacles of afflictions and karma] constitute obstacles to retribution, there is a distinction between suffering and pleasure.
The three evil realms consist solely of suffering and are obtained by transgressing the Dharma; therefore, the performance of ritual methods can eliminate them.
The retribution of the human realm consists of half suffering and half joy; it is summoned by scattered wholesome deeds, and thus can be extinguished by grasping signs.

The celestial retribution within the three realms, compared to that of humans, is entirely fixed; there is no suffering, only joy, and it is induced by the three outflows; therefore, it can be extinguished by the state of non-arising.
4. From "Furthermore" (*yòu*) onwards, the explanation excludes the three types of karma.
The retributions can be understood by analogy; these two explanations are distinguished based on the distinction between that which evokes retribution and that which is evoked.
2. From "Furthermore, [if one] acts" (*yòu zuò*) onwards, there are two sections, which are exclusively the Great Explanation (*dà shì*).

The previous four explanations encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; they do not distinguish between the general and specific regarding the non-arising of delusions, and their methods of practice may adopt the regulations of the Vinaya.

The present two explanations concern the non-arising of the ignorance that constitutes the obstacle within the state of cessation; that the general delusions do not arise is what is taken as the characteristic here.
Examining this departure, it pertains solely to the Great Śākya [Buddha]. It has two parts:
first, the individual explanations of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fear belongs to volition (*cetanā*), while sorrow and grief belong to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Now, when the ritual is completed, one resides in the fifth stage (*pañcamī-bhūmi*) and is able to subdue these delusions.
Since "subduing" is here designated as "destroying," it is said that this [stage] also achieves it.

When the ritual of grasping signs is completed, one resides in the stage of the seven levels of faith (*saptādhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and thus the four abiding delusions (*catur-vāsana*) are extinguished.
Having already seen the True Reality (satyadharma), one regards names and marks as being within [that reality]; therefore, this is called "taking marks.

When the contemplation of non-arising is perfected, one ascends to the first stage (bhūmi). What is specifically eliminated at this point is fundamental ignorance (mūlāvidyā); thus, we know that this explanation specifically elucidates the three types of repentance according to the Mahāyāna.
2. From "Furthermore, there are three" onwards, the explanation is given by way of the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Regarding "collectively removing retribution": this refers to present retribution.

That the body born of one's parents attains the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*) is the actual transformation of retribution; it truly requires the combined practice of the primary and auxiliary methods.

If one practices only through principle-contemplation (*li-guan*), although one may enter the true or semblance stages, there are still those who do not attain the purity of the six sense organs; therefore, it is said that the three types of repentance together remove the obstacle of retribution (*bao-zhang*).
As for "removing karma by grasping signs" (*qu-xiang chu-ye*), this is explained in terms of emerging into the provisional (*chu-jia*).

Being able to take up the immeasurable karmic seeds from past lives to serve as conditions for delivering sentient beings, such that karma cannot act as an obstruction and one attains mastery over karma, is called "removing karmic obstructions.

Because this stage is not yet the true position of emerging into the provisional (the *niṣyanda-nirmāṇa*), seeing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is still termed "grasping at marks" (*nimitta-grāha*).
The meaning of "eliminating delusions through non-arising" can be understood.
Second, from the phrase "furthermore, it acts" onwards, the cultivation of wholesome qualities is clarified;
this is still explained by means of a metaphor.
The five minerals refer to white crystal, purple crystal, gypsum, stalactite, and bitumen.
The five fungi refer to the five-colored lingzhi mushrooms.
The ginger and cassia serve as metaphors for the ritual practices of the Hīnayāna; therefore, they do not yet give rise to goodness.
If one performs great rituals, the goodness produced is no small amount.
The five stones and five fungi collectively serve as metaphors for the production of both mundane and supramundane, phenomenal and noumenal goodness, within both the Small and Great Vehicles.
2. From "In this way" onwards, there is an exhortation for others to practice and study.

The phrase "one must know" means that one must know that both the Small and Great [Vehicles] are capable of extinguishing evil and generating goodness; one must know that these three practices are beneficial only when cultivated. To merely speak of them without practicing them results in the acquisition of transgression.
III. "Now, the Text" below clarifies that the Sūtra contains three types of repentance; this section has two parts:
first, showing that the Sūtra has three textual passages;
second, concluding that repentance serves as the function of the Sūtra.
